claim: Mice missing the Complex I subunit NADH dehydrogenase [ubiquinone] iron-sulfur protein 4 (NDUFS4) are a leading mammalian model of severe mitochondrial disease.
source: Mice missing the Complex I subunit NADH dehydrogenase [ubiquinone] iron-sulfur protein 4 (NDUFS4) are a leading mammalian model of severe mitochondrial disease that exhibit many characteristic symptoms of Leigh Syndrome including oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, brain lesions, and premature death.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature establishing this mouse model.

claim: NDUFS4 knockout mice exhibit many characteristic symptoms of Leigh Syndrome including oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, brain lesions, and premature death.
source: Mice missing the Complex I subunit NADH dehydrogenase [ubiquinone] iron-sulfur protein 4 (NDUFS4) are a leading mammalian model of severe mitochondrial disease that exhibit many characteristic symptoms of Leigh Syndrome including oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, brain lesions, and premature death.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and is consistent with the experimental observations in this manuscript.

claim: NDUFS4 knockout mice have decreased expression of nearly every Complex I subunit.
source: NDUFS4 knockout mice have decreased expression of nearly every Complex I subunit.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors (Martin-Perez et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2013).

claim: Complex I normally contains at least 8 iron-sulfur clusters and more than 25 iron atoms.
source: As Complex I normally contains at least 8 iron-sulfur clusters and more than 25 iron atoms, we asked whether a deficiency of Complex I may lead to iron perturbations, thereby accelerating disease progression.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Complex I structure.

claim: Iron supplementation accelerates symptoms of brain degeneration in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: Consistent with this, iron supplementation accelerates symptoms of brain degeneration in these mice, while iron restriction delays the onset of these symptoms, reduces neuroinflammation, and increases survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that iron-dextran injection accelerated the onset of clasping (Figure 1D).

claim: Iron restriction delays the onset of symptoms in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: Consistent with this, iron supplementation accelerates symptoms of brain degeneration in these mice, while iron restriction delays the onset of these symptoms, reduces neuroinflammation, and increases survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing delayed clasping onset with low iron diet (Figure 1D).

claim: Iron restriction reduces neuroinflammation in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: Consistent with this, iron supplementation accelerates symptoms of brain degeneration in these mice, while iron restriction delays the onset of these symptoms, reduces neuroinflammation, and increases survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced GFAP expression in iron-restricted mice (Figure 3D and E).

claim: Iron restriction increases survival in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: Consistent with this, iron supplementation accelerates symptoms of brain degeneration in these mice, while iron restriction delays the onset of these symptoms, reduces neuroinflammation, and increases survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased median lifespan with low iron diet (Figure 1E).

claim: NDUFS4 knockout mice display signs of iron overload in the liver including increased expression of hepcidin.
source: NDUFS4 knockout mice display signs of iron overload in the liver including increased expression of hepcidin and show changes in iron-responsive element-regulated proteins consistent with increased cellular iron that were prevented by iron restriction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing increased Hamp1 mRNA in liver (Figure 5F).

claim: NDUFS4 knockout mice show changes in iron-responsive element-regulated proteins consistent with increased cellular iron.
source: NDUFS4 knockout mice display signs of iron overload in the liver including increased expression of hepcidin and show changes in iron-responsive element-regulated proteins consistent with increased cellular iron that were prevented by iron restriction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing changes in FTH1, TFR1, and other IRE-regulated proteins (Figure 4).

claim: Iron restriction prevents changes in iron-responsive element-regulated proteins in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: NDUFS4 knockout mice display signs of iron overload in the liver including increased expression of hepcidin and show changes in iron-responsive element-regulated proteins consistent with increased cellular iron that were prevented by iron restriction.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing normalization of IRE-regulated protein expression with low iron diet (Figure 4 and Figure 5).

claim: Perturbed iron homeostasis may contribute to pathology in Leigh Syndrome.
source: These results suggest that perturbed iron homeostasis may contribute to pathology in Leigh Syndrome and possibly other mitochondrial disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings in the mouse model.

claim: Perturbed iron homeostasis may contribute to pathology in other mitochondrial disorders.
source: These results suggest that perturbed iron homeostasis may contribute to pathology in Leigh Syndrome and possibly other mitochondrial disorders.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings in the mouse model.

claim: Reduced assembly and/or activity of respiratory Complex I or other complexes of the electron transport chain are widely implicated in the etiology of most mitochondrial diseases.
source: Reduced assembly and/or activity of respiratory Complex I or other complexes of the electron transport chain (ETC) are widely implicated in the etiology of most of these mitochondrial diseases (Stenton and Prokisch, 2020; Wallace, 2005; Nunnari and Suomalainen, 2012; Chan, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Decreased oxidative phosphorylation through aberrant ETC function is a common feature of age-related diseases including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, heart disease, and diabetes.
source: Additionally, a common feature of age-related diseases, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease (PD), heart disease, and diabetes, is decreased oxidative phosphorylation through aberrant ETC function (Kaeberlein, 2017; Kaeberlein et al., 2015; Kennedy et al., 2014; López-Otín et al., 2013; Shigenaga et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Complex I is the largest of the ETC complexes and is made up of 45 subunit proteins.
source: Complex I is the largest of the ETC complexes and is made up of 45 subunit proteins that represent a considerable portion of the protein mass of the inner mitochondrial membrane (Hirst, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Hirst, 2013).

claim: Complex I coordinates the transfer of electrons from NADH to ubiquinone via a shuttle of eight or more redox-active iron-sulfur clusters found on the peripheral arm in the mitochondrial matrix.
source: It coordinates the transfer of electrons from NADH to ubiquinone via a shuttle of eight or more redox-active iron-sulfur clusters found on the peripheral arm in the mitochondrial matrix, but little is known on the effects of improper regulation, assembly, biogenesis, and dynamics of these iron-sulfur clusters in the pathophysiology of Complex I deficiencies.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Complex I function.

claim: Leigh Syndrome is characterized by lactic acidosis, neuroinflammation, brain lesions of the basal ganglia, and death within the first few years of life.
source: One of the most prevalent hereditary mitochondrial diseases is Leigh Syndrome, which is characterized by lactic acidosis, neuroinflammation, brain lesions of the basal ganglia, and death within the first few years of life (Darin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Darin et al., 2001).

claim: Nearly 35% of Leigh Syndrome cases can be caused by various mutations affecting Complex I including NDUFS4 and several other iron-sulfur proteins on the redox-active peripheral arm.
source: Nearly 35% of Leigh Syndrome cases can be caused by various mutations affecting Complex I including NDUFS4 and several other iron-sulfur proteins on the redox-active peripheral arm (Stenton and Prokisch, 2020; Chang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Stenton and Prokisch, 2020; Chang et al., 2020).

claim: Mice missing the Complex I subunit NDUFS4 are a leading mammalian model of Leigh Syndrome.
source: Mice missing the Complex I subunit NDUFS4 are a leading mammalian model of Leigh Syndrome (Kruse et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Kruse et al., 2008).

claim: Knockout of the iron-sulfur protein NDUFS4 in mice decreases the expression of nearly all Complex I subunits.
source: We previously reported knockout of the iron-sulfur protein NDUFS4 (Ndufs4−/−) in mice decreases the expression of nearly all Complex I subunits, and we were unable to observe appreciable Complex I or respiratory supercomplex formation (Martin-Perez et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors (Martin-Perez et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2013).

claim: In NDUFS4 knockout mice, appreciable Complex I or respiratory supercomplex formation was not observed.
source: We previously reported knockout of the iron-sulfur protein NDUFS4 (Ndufs4−/−) in mice decreases the expression of nearly all Complex I subunits, and we were unable to observe appreciable Complex I or respiratory supercomplex formation (Martin-Perez et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors (Martin-Perez et al., 2020; Johnson et al., 2013).

claim: Iron-sulfur cluster deficiencies in cells have recently been linked to an accumulation of iron.
source: Iron-sulfur cluster deficiencies in cells have recently been linked to an accumulation of iron (Terzi et al., 2021), and prior evidence in cells suggests inhibition of Complex I with rotenone promotes iron accumulation that is dependent on iron sensor protein activity (Mena et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2020; Urrutia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Terzi et al., 2021).

claim: Inhibition of Complex I with rotenone promotes iron accumulation that is dependent on iron sensor protein activity.
source: Iron-sulfur cluster deficiencies in cells have recently been linked to an accumulation of iron (Terzi et al., 2021), and prior evidence in cells suggests inhibition of Complex I with rotenone promotes iron accumulation that is dependent on iron sensor protein activity (Mena et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2020; Urrutia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Mena et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2020; Urrutia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2009).

claim: Iron is the most biologically abundant transition metal.
source: Iron, as an essential nutrient, is the most biologically abundant transition metal that plays key roles in physiology (Hentze et al., 2010; Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011; Grillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and is established knowledge.

claim: Iron plays key roles in physiology.
source: Iron, as an essential nutrient, is the most biologically abundant transition metal that plays key roles in physiology (Hentze et al., 2010; Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011; Grillo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and is established knowledge.

claim: Iron is pervasively utilized as an enzymatic co-factor due to its unique readiness to undergo facile redox cycling in cellular milieu.
source: It is pervasively utilized as an enzymatic co-factor due to its unique readiness to undergo facile redox cycling in cellular milieu.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about iron chemistry and biology.

claim: Iron is largely localized to mitochondria due to its essential role in electron transfer during cellular respiration and in mitochondrial metabolism.
source: Iron is largely localized to mitochondria due to its essential role in electron transfer during cellular respiration and in mitochondrial metabolism (Pierrel et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Pierrel et al., 2007).

claim: The high reactivity of iron facilitates reactive oxygen species generation, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and organ damage when in excess.
source: The high reactivity of iron, however, facilitates reactive oxygen species generation, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, and organ damage when in excess (Valko et al., 2005; Stohs and Bagchi, 1995; Lieu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Valko et al., 2005; Stohs and Bagchi, 1995; Lieu et al., 2001).

claim: Iron homeostasis is tightly controlled through multiple transcriptional, translational, and post-translational iron-dependent feedback regulatory mechanisms such as the iron-responsive element (IRE) signaling pathway and the hepcidin-ferroportin axis.
source: Iron homeostasis is tightly controlled through multiple transcriptional, translational, and post-translational iron-dependent feedback regulatory mechanisms such as the iron-responsive element (IRE) signaling pathway and the hepcidin-ferroportin axis (Hentze et al., 2010; Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Hentze et al., 2010; Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011).

claim: Abnormal iron accumulation and/or utilization can overwhelm regulatory mechanisms leading to disease.
source: However, abnormal iron accumulation and/or utilization can overwhelm these regulatory mechanisms leading to disease (Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011).

claim: There is a high correlation between the onset of clasping and observed lifespan in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: There is a high correlation between the onset of clasping and observed lifespan (Figure 1A), making this neurobehavioral symptom an appropriate readout of disease progression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A with p=0.0047 by Pearson's test.

claim: Clasping is an appropriate readout of disease progression in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: There is a high correlation between the onset of clasping and observed lifespan (Figure 1A), making this neurobehavioral symptom an appropriate readout of disease progression.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation between clasping onset and lifespan.

claim: Control Ndufs4−/− mice fed standard chow began clasping around 40 days of age.
source: Control Ndufs4−/− mice fed standard chow began clasping around 40 days of age, consistent with our prior reports (Martin-Perez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work (Martin-Perez et al., 2020).

claim: Treatment with deferiprone delayed the onset of clasping in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: We observed treatment with this brain-penetrating iron chelator delayed the onset of clasping (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Deferiprone treatment increased median lifespan in Ndufs4−/− mice.
source: Deferiprone treatment also increased median lifespan in Ndufs4−/− mice (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Deferoxamine does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier.
source: The hydrophilic iron chelator deferoxamine does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier (Liu et al., 2005) and was used to ask whether brain iron chelation was necessary for the observed effects.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Liu et al., 2005).

claim: Deferoxamine treatment showed no changes on clasping or lifespan in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: In contrast to deferiprone, we observed no changes upon deferoxamine treatment on clasping or lifespan (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and D.

claim: Local iron chelation in the brain is critical for the observed effects of iron chelation on disease progression in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: This suggests that local iron chelation in the brain is critical for the observed effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of brain-penetrating deferiprone versus non-brain-penetrating deferoxamine.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a synthetic diet clasp at earlier ages than Ndufs4−/− mice fed standard chow diets.
source: It was reported that Ndufs4−/− mice fed a synthetic diet clasp at earlier ages and have shorter lifespans than Ndufs4−/− mice fed standard chow diets (Grillo et al., 2021), which we similarly observed (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Grillo et al., 2021) and experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a synthetic diet have shorter lifespans than Ndufs4−/− mice fed standard chow diets.
source: It was reported that Ndufs4−/− mice fed a synthetic diet clasp at earlier ages and have shorter lifespans than Ndufs4−/− mice fed standard chow diets (Grillo et al., 2021), which we similarly observed (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Grillo et al., 2021) and experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: High iron supplementation via intraperitoneal injection of iron-dextran accelerated the onset of clasping in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: High iron supplementation via intraperitoneal injection of iron-dextran (100 mg/kg every 3 days) accelerated the onset of clasping (Figure 1D), while feeding mice a low iron (8 ppm) synthetic diet dramatically delayed the onset of clasping without causing any significant deleterious changes in weight (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Feeding mice a low iron (8 ppm) synthetic diet dramatically delayed the onset of clasping without causing any significant deleterious changes in weight.
source: High iron supplementation via intraperitoneal injection of iron-dextran (100 mg/kg every 3 days) accelerated the onset of clasping (Figure 1D), while feeding mice a low iron (8 ppm) synthetic diet dramatically delayed the onset of clasping without causing any significant deleterious changes in weight (Figure 1D and F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and F.

claim: The delay in disease progression with low iron diet was associated with ~15% increase in lifespan in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: This delay in disease progression was associated with ~15% increase in lifespan (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed signs of microcytic, hypochromic anemia consistent with iron deficiency.
source: As expected, Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed signs of microcytic, hypochromic anemia consistent with iron deficiency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on hematological parameters (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed decreased hematocrit compared to normal iron diet cohorts.
source: We observed decreased hematocrit, reduced hemoglobin levels, and decreased red blood cell production in Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet compared to the normal iron diet cohorts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed reduced hemoglobin levels compared to normal iron diet cohorts.
source: We observed decreased hematocrit, reduced hemoglobin levels, and decreased red blood cell production in Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet compared to the normal iron diet cohorts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed decreased red blood cell production compared to normal iron diet cohorts.
source: We observed decreased hematocrit, reduced hemoglobin levels, and decreased red blood cell production in Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet compared to the normal iron diet cohorts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed decreases in mean corpuscular volume.
source: We also observed decreases in mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration with the low iron diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed decreases in mean corpuscular hemoglobin.
source: We also observed decreases in mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration with the low iron diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet showed decreases in mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration.
source: We also observed decreases in mean corpuscular volume, mean corpuscular hemoglobin, and mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration with the low iron diet (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Total liver iron levels tripled in Ndufs4−/− mice fed the control synthetic diet relative to WT mice.
source: ICP-MS of tissue digestates revealed that total liver iron levels tripled in Ndufs4−/− mice fed the control synthetic diet relative to WT mice (Figure 2A and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: Significantly decreased iron levels in kidney were observed in mice fed the low iron diet.
source: Significantly decreased iron levels in kidney and duodenum were observed in mice fed the low iron diet (Figure 2A–G and Table 1), and we observed a global reduction in iron levels in the tissues tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: Significantly decreased iron levels in duodenum were observed in mice fed the low iron diet.
source: Significantly decreased iron levels in kidney and duodenum were observed in mice fed the low iron diet (Figure 2A–G and Table 1), and we observed a global reduction in iron levels in the tissues tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and Table 1.

claim: A global reduction in iron levels was observed in the tissues tested in mice fed the low iron diet.
source: Significantly decreased iron levels in kidney and duodenum were observed in mice fed the low iron diet (Figure 2A–G and Table 1), and we observed a global reduction in iron levels in the tissues tested (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Iron restriction did not affect the relative weights of tissues compared to mice fed the control diet.
source: Iron restriction did not affect the relative weights of these tissues compared to mice fed the control diet (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: No differences in total iron in whole brain digestates were observed from 35-day-old WT and Ndufs4−/− mice fed the normal or low iron diets.
source: We observed no differences in total iron in whole brain digestates from 35-day-old WT and Ndufs4−/− mice fed the normal or low iron diets (Figure 2B and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Elevated manganese levels were observed in WT and Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet in the liver, brain, kidney, and other tissues relative to control mice.
source: Consistent with the putative effect that iron restriction has on increasing manganese uptake, we observed elevated manganese levels in WT and Ndufs4−/− mice fed a low iron diet in the liver, brain, kidney, and other tissues relative to control mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Table 1.

claim: Control Ndufs4−/− mice had increased basal manganese levels compared to WT cohorts.
source: The control Ndufs4−/− mice had increased basal manganese levels compared to WT cohorts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Table 1.

claim: Increased basal manganese levels in control Ndufs4−/− mice may be due to a compensatory upregulation of mitochondrial manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase (MnSOD aka SOD2) to combat iron-mediated oxidative stress.
source: This may be due to a compensatory upregulation of mitochondrial manganese-dependent superoxide dismutase (MnSOD aka SOD2) to combat iron-mediated oxidative stress when mice were fed the normal iron diet (Lee et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to prior literature (Lee et al., 2019).

claim: No notable changes in copper, zinc, or other biorelevant metals were observed in iron-restricted mice.
source: We did not observe any notable changes in copper, zinc, or other biorelevant metals in iron-restricted mice (Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Table 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice fed the normal iron diet showed increased copper levels relative to control WT mice.
source: However, Ndufs4−/− mice fed the normal iron diet showed increased copper levels relative to control WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice have been reported to have elevated, and presumably toxic, levels of oxygen in the brain, blood, and other tissues due to their decreased respiratory activity.
source: Ndufs4−/− mice have been reported to have elevated, and presumably toxic, levels of oxygen in the brain, blood, and other tissues due to their decreased respiratory activity (Jain et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Livers from Ndufs4−/− mice on the control iron diet had increased non-heme iron.
source: Consistent with this, we observed livers from Ndufs4−/− mice on the control iron diet had increased non-heme iron (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A non-significant trend toward higher MDA levels was observed in livers from control Ndufs4−/− mice compared to WT cohorts.
source: We observed a non-significant trend toward higher MDA levels in livers from control Ndufs4−/− mice compared to WT cohorts (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A strong correlation was observed between the length of time Ndufs4−/− mice exhibited neurodegenerative symptoms (i.e., clasping) and observed MDA levels.
source: We observed a strong correlation between the length of time Ndufs4−/− mice exhibited neurodegenerative symptoms (i.e., clasping) and observed MDA levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C with p=0.0152 by Pearson's test.

claim: Iron-deficient mice showed decreased MDA levels.
source: Iron-deficient mice showed decreased MDA levels (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Iron accumulation in livers of Ndufs4−/− mice promotes oxidative stress.
source: Collectively, this data support the hypothesis that iron accumulation in livers of Ndufs4−/− mice promotes oxidative stress.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on non-heme iron, MDA levels, and their correlation with disease symptoms.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice normally exhibit neuroinflammation and brain lesions in the olfactory bulb, cerebellum, and brain stem around the onset of clasping.
source: Ndufs4−/− mice normally exhibit neuroinflammation and brain lesions in the olfactory bulb, cerebellum, and brain stem around the onset of clasping, while other brain regions are largely unaffected (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Johnson et al., 2020).

claim: Other brain regions are largely unaffected in Ndufs4−/− mice.
source: Ndufs4−/− mice normally exhibit neuroinflammation and brain lesions in the olfactory bulb, cerebellum, and brain stem around the onset of clasping, while other brain regions are largely unaffected (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Johnson et al., 2020).

claim: No significant differences in the astrogliosis marker GFAP were observed in whole brain extracts.
source: We did not observe significant differences in the astrogliosis marker GFAP in whole brain extracts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (implied from the text and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).

claim: Increased GFAP expression was observed in the olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Ndufs4−/− mice fed the control iron diet.
source: However, we observed increased GFAP expression in the olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Ndufs4−/− mice fed the control iron diet while GFAP levels in the cortex were unchanged (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: GFAP levels in the cortex were unchanged in Ndufs4−/− mice fed the control iron diet.
source: However, we observed increased GFAP expression in the olfactory bulb and cerebellum of Ndufs4−/− mice fed the control iron diet while GFAP levels in the cortex were unchanged (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: GFAP levels were reduced in the olfactory bulb and cerebellum in iron-restricted mice.
source: Consistent with the capacity for iron restriction to delay clasping (Figure 1D), GFAP levels were reduced in these regions in iron-restricted mice (Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: Body iron distribution is solely controlled by regulating iron absorption, metabolism, and storage as there are no known adaptive biological mechanisms for iron excretion.
source: Body iron distribution is solely controlled by regulating iron absorption, metabolism, and storage as there are no known adaptive biological mechanisms for iron excretion (Lieu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Lieu et al., 2001).

claim: The expression of iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) is highly sensitive to intracellular iron perturbations.
source: The expression of iron regulatory proteins (IRPs) is highly sensitive to intracellular iron perturbations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about iron regulatory proteins.

claim: Upregulation of the iron storage protein ferritin helps reduce cellular labile iron and avoid oxidative stress in cases of iron overload.
source: For example, upregulation of the iron storage protein ferritin helps reduce cellular labile iron and avoid oxidative stress in cases of iron overload.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ferritin function.

claim: Regulation of iron regulatory proteins is primarily achieved at the translational and post-translational levels through IREs and the hepcidin-ferroportin axis.
source: Regulation is primarily achieved at the translational and post-translational levels through IREs and the hepcidin-ferroportin axis (Hentze et al., 2010; Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Hentze et al., 2010; Bleackley and Macgillivray, 2011).

claim: Expression of the cytosolic iron storage protein ferritin is controlled by 5′-IREs found on its 24 heavy (Fth1) and light (Ftl1) chain subunits.
source: Expression of the cytosolic iron storage protein ferritin is controlled by 5′-IREs found on its 24 heavy (Fth1) and light (Ftl1) chain subunits and is an excellent readout of free cellular iron.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ferritin regulation.

claim: Ferritin is an excellent readout of free cellular iron.
source: Expression of the cytosolic iron storage protein ferritin is controlled by 5′-IREs found on its 24 heavy (Fth1) and light (Ftl1) chain subunits and is an excellent readout of free cellular iron.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ferritin as an iron status marker.

claim: Ferritin can deposit more than 4000 iron atoms into its central core.
source: Ferritin can deposit more than 4000 iron atoms into its central core, thereby acting as an iron sponge (Harrison and Arosio, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Harrison and Arosio, 1996).

claim: In cases of iron overload, IRPs dissociate from the 5′-IRE allowing for translation of FTH1 and FTL1.
source: In cases of iron overload, IRPs dissociate from the 5′-IRE allowing for translation of FTH1 and FTL1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IRE regulation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockout of NDUFS4 increased FTH1 protein expression in liver.
source: Consistent with iron overload in livers of control Ndufs4−/− mice, we observed knockout of NDUFS4 increased FTH1 protein expression (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Iron restriction in Ndufs4−/− mice downregulated FTH1 expression.
source: Iron restriction in Ndufs4−/− mice downregulated FTH1 expression, consistent with iron deficiency anemia (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Tfr1 mRNA contains a 3′-IRE and is normally expressed at high levels with iron restriction.
source: Transferrin Receptor 1 (TFR1) mediates the cellular internalization of iron-bound transferrin. Tfr1 mRNA contains a 3′-IRE and is normally expressed at high levels with iron restriction.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about TFR1 regulation.

claim: To adapt to iron overload, IRPs dissociate from the Tfr1 mRNA leading to its endonuclease-mediated degradation.
source: To adapt to iron overload, IRPs dissociate from the Tfr1 mRNA leading to its endonuclease-mediated degradation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about IRE regulation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Control Ndufs4−/− mice showed decreased levels of Tfr1 mRNA in liver by qRT-PCR relative to WT mice.
source: Control Ndufs4−/− mice showed decreased levels of Tfr1 mRNA in liver by qRT-PCR relative to WT mice (Figure 5A), consistent with increased labile iron in the mitochondrial disease mice.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Decreased Tfr1 mRNA in control Ndufs4−/− mice is consistent with increased labile iron.
source: Control Ndufs4−/− mice showed decreased levels of Tfr1 mRNA in liver by qRT-PCR relative to WT mice (Figure 5A), consistent with increased labile iron in the mitochondrial disease mice.

claim: Upregulation of Tfr1 mRNA and TFR1 protein was observed in livers from the WT and Ndufs4−/− mice fed the low iron diet.
source: As expected, we observed upregulation of Tfr1 mRNA and TFR1 protein in livers from the WT and Ndufs4−/− mice fed the low iron diet (Figure 4 and Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5A.

claim: Changes in other IRE-regulated genes at the mRNA or protein level in liver were observed as expected for IRE-dependent regulation.
source: We also observed changes in other IRE-regulated genes at the mRNA or protein level in liver as expected for IRE-dependent regulation (Figure 4 and Figure 5A–E).

claim: Iron deficiency in Ndufs4−/− mice prevented the altered expression of IRE-regulated genes.

claim: No appreciable differences in FTH1 or TFR1 expression were observed in the brain.

claim: Hepcidin is a liver-derived master regulator of iron absorption, iron recycling, iron storage, and in erythropoiesis.
source: The peptide hepcidin is a liver-derived master regulator of iron absorption, iron recycling, iron storage, and in erythropoiesis (Hentze et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Hentze et al., 2010).

claim: In situations of excess iron, hepatic production and systemic circulation of hepcidin promote ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the iron export protein ferroportin (FPN1).
source: In situations of excess iron, hepatic production and systemic circulation of hepcidin promote ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the iron export protein ferroportin (FPN1), thereby trapping iron in duodenal epithelia and in liver macrophages.

claim: Hepcidin-mediated degradation of FPN1 traps iron in duodenal epithelia and in liver macrophages.
source: In situations of excess iron, hepatic production and systemic circulation of hepcidin promote ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the iron export protein ferroportin (FPN1), thereby trapping iron in duodenal epithelia and in liver macrophages.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the hepcidin-ferroportin axis.

claim: Hepcidin promotes the storage of excess iron in the liver and reduces iron absorption from the diet as an effective adaptive mechanism protecting against iron-mediated damage in cases of iron overload.
source: This promotes the storage of excess iron in the liver and reduces iron absorption from the diet as an effective adaptive mechanism protecting against iron-mediated damage in cases of iron overload.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about hepcidin function.

claim: Fpn1 mRNA contains a 5′-IRE.
source: While Fpn1 mRNA contains a 5′-IRE, hepcidin-mediated degradation of FPN1 prevents its IRE-dependent upregulation in the liver or gut epithelia with iron overload.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Fpn1 regulation.

claim: Hepcidin-mediated degradation of FPN1 prevents its IRE-dependent upregulation in the liver or gut epithelia with iron overload.
source: While Fpn1 mRNA contains a 5′-IRE, hepcidin-mediated degradation of FPN1 prevents its IRE-dependent upregulation in the liver or gut epithelia with iron overload.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the interplay between hepcidin and IRE regulation.

claim: No significant increases in FPN1 protein were observed in Ndufs4−/− liver.
source: Consistent with this, we did not observe significant increases in FPN1 protein in Ndufs4−/− liver (Figure 4).

claim: Transcript levels of Hamp1 increased twofold in livers of control Ndufs4−/− mice.
source: Transcript levels of Hamp1 increased twofold in livers of control Ndufs4−/− mice, further consistent with our ferritin data suggesting increased hepatic iron stores.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Increased Hamp1 transcript levels in control Ndufs4−/− mice is consistent with increased hepatic iron stores.
source: Transcript levels of Hamp1 increased twofold in livers of control Ndufs4−/− mice, further consistent with our ferritin data suggesting increased hepatic iron stores.
evidence: This is inferred from the known regulation of hepcidin by iron status.

claim: Iron restriction drastically downregulated Hamp1 transcription in liver to nearly undetectable levels.
source: Iron restriction drastically downregulated Hamp1 transcription in liver to nearly undetectable levels (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Iron is widely recognized as a critical mediator in the progression of many age-related and genetic neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Iron is widely recognized as a critical mediator in the progression of many age-related and genetic neurodegenerative diseases (Lieu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Lieu et al., 2001).

claim: Iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models accelerates the aggregation of alpha-synuclein.
source: For example, iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models accelerates the aggregation of alpha-synuclein, promotes free radical accumulation, increases lipid peroxidation, and is implicated in dementia and motor impairment (Zecca et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Zecca et al., 2004).

claim: Iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models promotes free radical accumulation.
source: For example, iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models accelerates the aggregation of alpha-synuclein, promotes free radical accumulation, increases lipid peroxidation, and is implicated in dementia and motor impairment (Zecca et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Zecca et al., 2004).

claim: Iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models increases lipid peroxidation.
source: For example, iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models accelerates the aggregation of alpha-synuclein, promotes free radical accumulation, increases lipid peroxidation, and is implicated in dementia and motor impairment (Zecca et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Zecca et al., 2004).

claim: Iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models is implicated in dementia and motor impairment.
source: For example, iron deposition in the basal ganglia of PD patients and mouse models accelerates the aggregation of alpha-synuclein, promotes free radical accumulation, increases lipid peroxidation, and is implicated in dementia and motor impairment (Zecca et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Zecca et al., 2004).

claim: Treatment with the Complex I inhibitor rotenone is widely used as a PD model that reproduces many features including oxidative damage, dopaminergic degeneration in the substantia nigra, and Lewy Body inclusions.
source: Treatment with the Complex I inhibitor rotenone is widely used as a PD model that reproduces many features including oxidative damage, dopaminergic degeneration in the substantia nigra, and Lewy Body inclusions (Liang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Liang et al., 2020).

claim: Rotenone treatment increases the mitochondrial and cytosolic labile iron pool in neurons in vitro and in animal models.
source: Rotenone treatment increases the mitochondrial and cytosolic labile iron pool in neurons in vitro and in animal models (Mena et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2020; Urrutia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Mena et al., 2011; Liang et al., 2020; Urrutia et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2009).

claim: Point mutations of the Complex III chaperone ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase complex chaperone (BCS1L) can cause GRACILE syndrome.
source: For example, point mutations of the Complex III chaperone ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase complex chaperone (BCS1L) can cause the rare hereditary disease GRACILE (Growth Retardation, Aminoaciduria, Cholestasis, Iron overload, Lactic acidosis, and Early death) syndrome (Visapää et al., 2002; Fellman et al., 1998; Fellman, 2002; Fellman et al., 2008; Levéen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Visapää et al., 2002; Fellman et al., 1998; Fellman, 2002; Fellman et al., 2008; Levéen et al., 2011).

claim: BCS1L normally mediates the transfer of Rieske iron-sulfur protein into the pre-assembled Complex III dimer.
source: BCS1L normally mediates the transfer of Rieske iron-sulfur protein into the pre-assembled Complex III dimer, but its deficiency leads to elevated liver iron, increased serum iron or ferritin, and hypotransferrinemia (Visapää et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Visapää et al., 2002).

claim: BCS1L deficiency leads to elevated liver iron, increased serum iron or ferritin, and hypotransferrinemia.
source: BCS1L normally mediates the transfer of Rieske iron-sulfur protein into the pre-assembled Complex III dimer, but its deficiency leads to elevated liver iron, increased serum iron or ferritin, and hypotransferrinemia (Visapää et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Visapää et al., 2002).

claim: There is considerable overlap between the metabolic alterations in patients with Leigh Syndrome and GRACILE syndrome.
source: There is considerable overlap between the metabolic alterations in patients with Leigh Syndrome and GRACILE syndrome.
evidence: This is inferred from the discussion of shared features between the two syndromes.

claim: Some mutations of BCS1L cause Leigh Syndrome (e.g., P99L).
source: This is demonstrated by findings that some mutations of BCS1L cause Leigh Syndrome (e.g., P99L) (de Lonlay et al., 2001), while other mutations in this protein alternatively cause GRACILE syndrome (e.g., S78G) (Fellman et al., 2008).

claim: Other mutations in BCS1L alternatively cause GRACILE syndrome (e.g., S78G).
source: This is demonstrated by findings that some mutations of BCS1L cause Leigh Syndrome (e.g., P99L) (de Lonlay et al., 2001), while other mutations in this protein alternatively cause GRACILE syndrome (e.g., S78G) (Fellman et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Fellman et al., 2008).

claim: Shared metabolic changes between Leigh Syndrome and GRACILE syndrome include decreased respiratory supercomplex formation, reduced O2 consumption, high amino acid levels, NAD+ dyshomeostasis, increased glycolysis, and increased lactate fermentation.
source: Similar metabolic changes include decreased respiratory supercomplex formation, reduced O2 consumption, high amino acid levels, NAD+ dyshomeostasis, increased glycolysis, and increased lactate fermentation (Visapää et al., 2002; Fellman et al., 1998; Fellman, 2002; Fellman et al., 2008; Levéen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Visapää et al., 2002; Fellman et al., 1998; Fellman, 2002; Fellman et al., 2008; Levéen et al., 2011).

claim: GRACILE Syndrome patients with encephalopathy experience seizures, developmental delays, and other neurodegenerative symptoms.
source: As seen in Leigh Syndrome, GRACILE Syndrome patients with encephalopathy experience seizures, developmental delays, and other neurodegenerative symptoms (de Lonlay et al., 2001; Morris et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (de Lonlay et al., 2001; Morris et al., 1995).

claim: Shared phenotypic manifestations of Leigh and GRACILE Syndrome may be a result of overlapping pathophysiology of iron accumulation.
source: These shared phenotypic manifestations of Leigh and GRACILE Syndrome may be a result of overlapping pathophysiology of iron accumulation.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observed similarities between the syndromes.

claim: The liver plays a central role in iron absorption, metabolism, and regulation by acting as the primary iron storage vessel to protect sensitive organs, such as the brain.
source: The liver plays a central role in iron absorption, metabolism, and regulation by acting as the primary iron storage vessel to protect sensitive organs, such as the brain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about liver function in iron homeostasis.

claim: The liver promotes the controlled release of iron into the blood to maintain non-toxic physiological levels.
source: The liver promotes the controlled release of iron into the blood to maintain non-toxic physiological levels, is largely responsible for synthesizing circulating iron-binding proteins such as transferrin, and produces hepcidin—the master regulating peptide of iron absorption—in response to changes in hepatic iron stores (Hentze et al., 2010; Lieu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Hentze et al., 2010; Lieu et al., 2001).

claim: The liver is largely responsible for synthesizing circulating iron-binding proteins such as transferrin.
source: The liver promotes the controlled release of iron into the blood to maintain non-toxic physiological levels, is largely responsible for synthesizing circulating iron-binding proteins such as transferrin, and produces hepcidin—the master regulating peptide of iron absorption—in response to changes in hepatic iron stores (Hentze et al., 2010; Lieu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Hentze et al., 2010; Lieu et al., 2001).

claim: The liver produces hepcidin in response to changes in hepatic iron stores.
source: The liver promotes the controlled release of iron into the blood to maintain non-toxic physiological levels, is largely responsible for synthesizing circulating iron-binding proteins such as transferrin, and produces hepcidin—the master regulating peptide of iron absorption—in response to changes in hepatic iron stores (Hentze et al., 2010; Lieu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Hentze et al., 2010; Lieu et al., 2001).

claim: There is an excess of body iron in the setting of Complex I deficiency in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: Because of the liver's critical importance in maintaining systemic iron, our results suggest there is an excess of body iron in the setting of this Complex I deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed liver iron accumulation and changes in iron regulatory proteins.

claim: Liver-specific knockout of S6K1, but not neuronal S6K1, can delay the onset of disease and prolong survival in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: While the Ndufs4−/− mice experience a severe neurometabolic disease, we previously reported that liver-specific knockout of S6K1, but not neuronal S6K1, can delay the onset of disease and prolong survival (Ito et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors (Ito et al., 2017).

claim: Aberrations in liver physiology are implicated in Ndufs4−/− mouse disease progression that may translate to patients with Leigh Syndrome.
source: Our data further implicate aberrations in liver physiology in Ndufs4−/− mouse disease progression that may translate to patients with Leigh Syndrome.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The lack of noticeable differences in iron in whole brain digestates by ICP-MS may be due to well-controlled brain-specific adaptive mechanisms that limit iron absorption through the blood-brain barrier.
source: The reason for this is unclear, however, it may be due to well-controlled brain-specific adaptive mechanisms that limit iron absorption through the blood-brain barrier (Mills et al., 2010), or due to differential iron distribution in regions that are unaffected in Ndufs4−/− mice (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to prior literature (Mills et al., 2010).

claim: The lack of noticeable differences in iron in whole brain digestates by ICP-MS may be due to differential iron distribution in regions that are unaffected in Ndufs4−/− mice.
source: The reason for this is unclear, however, it may be due to well-controlled brain-specific adaptive mechanisms that limit iron absorption through the blood-brain barrier (Mills et al., 2010), or due to differential iron distribution in regions that are unaffected in Ndufs4−/− mice (Johnson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to prior literature (Johnson et al., 2020).

claim: Mice missing the iron regulatory protein IRP2 show neurocognitive deficits consistent with brain iron overload.
source: For example, mice missing the iron regulatory protein IRP2 show neurocognitive deficits consistent with brain iron overload, but iron is only deposited in glial cells and white matter while neuronal iron contrastingly decreases (Zumbrennen-Bullough et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Zumbrennen-Bullough et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2015).

claim: In IRP2 knockout mice, iron is only deposited in glial cells and white matter while neuronal iron contrastingly decreases.
source: For example, mice missing the iron regulatory protein IRP2 show neurocognitive deficits consistent with brain iron overload, but iron is only deposited in glial cells and white matter while neuronal iron contrastingly decreases (Zumbrennen-Bullough et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Zumbrennen-Bullough et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2015).

claim: Age-progressive iron accumulation is primarily found in the basal ganglia and other regions that control motor function while whole brain iron deposition is largely unchanged.
source: Age-progressive iron accumulation is primarily found in the basal ganglia and other regions that control motor function while whole brain iron deposition is largely unchanged (Ward et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Ward et al., 2014).

claim: Ndufs4−/− pathology is commonly observed in the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and olfactory bulbs.
source: In support of this, Ndufs4−/− pathology is commonly observed in the basal ganglia, cerebellum, and olfactory bulbs.

claim: Brain regions where Ndufs4−/− pathology is commonly observed tend to have higher iron levels than other regions.
source: These brain regions tend to have higher iron levels than other regions (Zecca et al., 2004; Ward et al., 2014).

claim: Iron does not need to cross the blood-brain barrier to accumulate in the olfactory bulb or brain stem.
source: Iron does not need to cross the blood-brain barrier to accumulate in the olfactory bulb or brain stem, and as such these regions are more sensitive to disturbances in iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about brain anatomy and the blood-brain barrier.

claim: The olfactory bulb and brain stem are more sensitive to disturbances in iron homeostasis.
source: Iron does not need to cross the blood-brain barrier to accumulate in the olfactory bulb or brain stem, and as such these regions are more sensitive to disturbances in iron homeostasis.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that iron does not need to cross the blood-brain barrier to reach these regions.

claim: Dietary iron restriction and treatment with an iron chelator both delay the onset of neurological symptoms (i.e., clasping) in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: We observed that dietary iron restriction, and treatment with an iron chelator, both delay the onset of neurological symptoms (i.e., clasping).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Altered whole body iron status can influence neurodegeneration in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: This is consistent with the idea that altered whole body iron status can influence neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the effects of dietary iron manipulation on neurological symptoms.

claim: It is unclear whether changes in organ function upon iron perturbation contribute to the observed effects on neurodegeneration.
source: However, it is unclear whether changes in organ function upon iron perturbation contribute to the observed effects.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in understanding the mechanism.

claim: It is possible that the speciation of iron is altered in NDUFS4 knockout mice.
source: Our data do not elucidate the specific forms or oxidation state of cellular iron that accumulates in Ndufs4−/− mice, but it is possible that the speciation of iron is altered.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging a limitation of the study.

claim: Complex I deficiency could alter the iron composition in the cell.
source: As Complex I normally utilizes >25 iron atoms in its iron-sulfur clusters, its deficiency could alter the iron composition in the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the known iron content of Complex I.

claim: Excess cellular labile iron is widely associated with ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, or other damaging processes.
source: In contrast to protein-bound iron, excess cellular labile iron is widely associated with ROS generation, lipid peroxidation, oxidative stress, ferroptosis, or other damaging processes (Valko et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Valko et al., 2005).

claim: Increased iron, increased levels of the lipid peroxidation byproduct MDA, and changes in the IRE-associated proteins TFR1 and ferritin subunits collectively support increased free cytosolic iron in Ndufs4−/− mouse liver that is recognized by IRP1 and IRP2.

This data collectively support increased free cytosolic iron in Ndufs4−/− mouse liver that is recognized by IRP1 and IRP2.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined experimental data.

claim: Iron is especially localized to mitochondria due to its widespread use in energy production, metabolism, and normal ROS signaling.
source: Iron is especially localized to mitochondria due to its widespread use in energy production, metabolism, and normal ROS signaling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial iron.

claim: A large proportion of mitochondrial iron is normally utilized in oxidative phosphorylation.

evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial iron utilization.

claim: Complex I inhibition with rotenone increased both cytosolic and mitochondrial labile iron in SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells.

claim: Alterations in subcellular iron distribution remain an attractive avenue of pursuit in the setting of a Complex I deficiency.
source: As NDUFS4 is found in mitochondria, alterations in subcellular iron distribution remain an attractive avenue of pursuit in the setting of a Complex I deficiency.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice are hyperoxic and show increased PO2 levels in the brain and blood.
source: Recent reports provide some evidence that Ndufs4−/− mice are hyperoxic, show increased PO2 levels in the brain and blood, and have perturbed redox status (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Ndufs4−/− mice have perturbed redox status.

claim: Excess oxygen is implicated in disease etiology in Ndufs4−/− mice.

claim: Induction of severe anemia by regular early life phlebotomy every other day in combination with an iron-deficient diet is beneficial in Ndufs4−/− mice.
source: Induction of severe anemia by regular early life phlebotomy every other day in combination with an iron-deficient diet is similarly beneficial (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: The low iron diet may decrease oxygen tension to delay the onset of neurodegenerative symptoms in Ndufs4−/− mice.

claim: The extent of lifespan extension with a low iron diet is small in comparison to severe anemia by combining iron restriction with regular phlebotomy.
source: However, the extent of lifespan extension with a low iron diet is small in comparison to severe anemia by combining iron restriction with regular phlebotomy.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results of this study with prior literature.

claim: Both iron restriction and phlebotomy may be necessary to drastically reduce oxygen delivery to the brain in Ndufs4−/− mice.
source: Both may be necessary to drastically reduce oxygen delivery to the brain.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on comparing different interventions.

claim: Genetic activation of the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) regulatory pathway via knockout of prolyl hydroxylases, nestin, or Von Hippel-Lindau protein in Ndufs4−/− mice is detrimental.
source: It was previously reported that genetic activation of the hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) regulatory pathway via knockout of prolyl hydroxylases, nestin, or Von Hippel-Lindau protein in Ndufs4−/− mice is detrimental (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Median lifespan in control Ndufs4−/− mice decreases from 64 to 29 days in Ndufs4−/− Nes-Phd2−/− triple transgenic mice that display HIF activation.

evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature (Jain et al., 2019).

claim: Increased iron absorption via hyperactivation of hypoxia-inducible factors may partially explain the detrimental effect of HIF activation in Ndufs4−/− mice.

source: Proteins sensitive to changes in cellular iron, such as TFR1 and ferritin, change in response to this iron overload.

claim: Changes in TFR1 and ferritin in NDUFS4 knockout mice are consistent with an increase in labile iron that can be recognized by iron response proteins.

claim: Iron restriction causes anemia in NDUFS4 knockout mice.

source: Our data suggest that decreased Complex I activity with aging may help contribute to this neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation, and therapeutic interventions targeting genetic or age-progressive causes of Complex I deficiencies may be especially beneficial.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is critical to better understand the generality of pathogenic iron dyshomeostasis in Leigh Syndrome patients with specific mutations.

claim: This work may have broader implications in the development of diagnostic markers for Leigh Syndrome, in which serum iron, transferrin saturation, serum ferritin, or serum hepcidin can be readily analyzed clinically.
source: This work may have broader implications in the development of diagnostic markers for Leigh Syndrome, in which serum iron, transferrin saturation, serum ferritin, or serum hepcidin can be readily analyzed clinically.
